title: GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM & CUDA graphs - Aurora AI
summary: Deep technical profiling session focusing on GPU kernel selection, tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, CUDA Graphs for steady-state throughput, KV cache behavior, batching strategies and quantization impacts. Customer asked about VPC/on-prem readiness and deterministic latency for inference in production. Agreed to run a joint benchmark and share kernel-level traces and recommended config for Aurora's mixed short/long prompt workload.
next_steps: Redwood to share kernel selection trace (NVTX + CUPTI summary) and sample CUDA graph config by 2026-07-27
Aurora to provide representative prompt set and 24h traffic profile by 2026-07-28
Schedule pilot benchmark on Aurora's on-prem A100 cluster (two days) - target week of 2026-08-03
action_items: Diego: export and share NVTX trace and lightweight CUPTI summary - due 2026-07-27
Ravi: upload representative prompt dataset + traffic histogram to shared folder - due 2026-07-28
Maya: send pricing options for dedicated vs hosted pilot and attach SOC2/security pack - due 2026-07-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-22 15:00 PT | Duration ~58m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ravi (Aurora CTO), Lina (ML Infra), Omar (SRE), Sam (developer)

[00:00:00] Maya: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a deep dive on GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection and compare TensorRT-LLM and vLLM approaches. Diego will lead the technical profile. Feel free to interrupt.

[00:00:23] Ravi: Thanks. We care about predictable latency at 95th and cost. Workload is mixed — lots of short prompts (<=64 tokens) plus some long chat histories up to 2k. We have A100s on-prem and also use GCP for bursts.

[00:00:45] Diego: Great, that's the kind of distribution that influences kernel choices and caching. Quick agenda: show profiling artifacts (NVTX/CUPTI), kernel hot spots, CUDA Graph warmup strategy, KV cache behavior, and then tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) and vLLM-style runtimes. We'll also touch on quantization and VPC/on-prem caveats.

[00:01:15] Lina: Quick note — we need to maintain session-level privacy controls, and any on-prem solution must integrate with our KMS. Also SOC2 questions later.

[00:01:30] Diego: Yep noted, Maya will follow up on security pack. Starting with a sample NVTX trace. (screen share) You can see the timeline: memory allocs, kernel launches, and large peaks during attention and rotary ops.

[00:02:12] Diego: With native PyTorch kernels we see many small kernels serialized — lots of kernel launch overhead for short sequences. TRT-LLM reduces that by fusing attention/feed-forward into bigger kernels, dropping launch overhead and improving 95th percentile for short prompts.

[00:02:45] Omar: Is that the typical TensorRT optimization where they fuse MHA and FFN into single kernels? We saw similar in our RD but worried about flexibility with model changes.

[00:03:02] Diego: Exactly. TRT-LLM does aggressive fusion and kernel selection at compile time. The tradeoff: longer compile times and less runtime flexibility for per-request dynamic shapes. vLLM tends to use many smaller kernels but does continuous batching/async scheduling which helps throughput for concurrent requests.

[00:03:30] Sam: Sorry, quick question — for our mixed workload, will fusing hurt long-context cases? We hit memory pressure at 2k contexts.

[00:03:45] Diego: Good question. Fused kernels often use more temporary memory; TRT-LLM can be memory-hungry at scale. We profile memory usage in the CUPTI summary — you'll see spikes during the fused MLP. For long contexts we recommend hybrid routing: use a fused TRT path for short/latency-sensitive traffic and a vLLM-like path that uses KV cache streaming for long context where memory locality is critical.

[00:04:18] Ravi: Hybrid routing — how do you decide at runtime? Policy or heuristics?

[00:04:25] Diego: We support policy-based routing — latency SLOs, token budget, or request length. For example: requests < 128 tokens -> TRT-LLM; requests > 512 or with large KV -> vLLM path. We also fallback automatically when GPU memory gets constrained.

[00:04:50] Lina: That sounds promising. How about CUDA Graphs — we've read they remove launch overhead for steady-state workloads. But our traffic is bursty.

[00:05:05] Diego: CUDA Graphs are best when you can predefine a stable execution graph — i.e., similar batch sizes and sequence lengths. They dramatically reduce CPU overhead and improve tail latencies once warmed. In bursty situations, you can maintain a pool of warmed graphs for common shapes and fallback to dynamic kernels otherwise. The tradeoff is graph management complexity and extra memory for pre-allocated workspaces.

[00:05:35] [00:05:36] Omar: (muffled) Is warmup expensive?

[00:05:40] Diego: Warmup involves a few iterations to populate the graph and the KV cache; usually seconds for common shapes but if you need tens of thousand of shapes it's infeasible. That's why we recommend shape bucketing and intelligent batching.

[00:06:05] Maya: We ran a customer benchmark where CUDA graphs + TRT-LLM reduced 95p latency for chat-like short prompts by ~40% compared to baseline vLLM scheduling, but vLLM delivered higher overall tokens/sec for long-form generation due to more efficient KV cache streaming.

[00:06:30] Ravi: Can you show an example CUPTI / kernel table we saw in the doc earlier? The kernel names are cryptic in our trace.

[00:06:40] Diego: (screen share) Here's a kernel breakdown: multi_head_attn_fused, gelu_ffn_fused, layer_norm, cudnn_gemm_xx. The NVTX markers help correlate request IDs to kernels. Note: transcription or detection sometimes labels our internal names differently if the model is custom — you'll see mismatches.

[00:07:05] Lina: About KV cache — we're concerned about memory fragmentation and eviction policies. In vLLM we saw good prefix caching. How does Redwood handle shared KV across requests?

[00:07:22] Diego: Our runtime uses a KV cache manager that supports per-request prefix caching, shared prefix reuse, and pointer-based views to avoid copies where possible. For multi-tenant workloads we enforce per-tenant caps and LRU eviction for inactive sessions. For on-prem you can configure retention windows and memory caps via the deployment config.

[00:07:50] Sam: What about consistency? If a prefix is evicted mid-session, do you transparently reload from disk or fail?

[00:07:58] Diego: We prioritize correctness — if an active session's KV is evicted we will rehydrate from a persisted prefix store (if configured) or fall back to recomputing prefixes which adds latency. We surface metrics and alerts so you can tune retention.

[00:08:25] Ravi: Quantization — we have models in fp16 but evaluating int8 or 4-bit. How does quantization interact with kernel selection?

[00:08:35] Diego: Quantization affects both kernel math and memory. TRT-LLM has strong int8 paths with custom kernels that exploit TensorRT's optimizations; those kernels are different names and sometimes different memory layouts. vLLM-style runtimes often use quantized matmul libraries (cuBLASLt, fused custom) with different tradeoffs. In practice int8 can reduce memory and increase throughput but may increase latency variance due to dequant/dequant steps unless fused.

[00:09:05] Lina: We ran 4-bit quantization with QKV reordering and saw quality regressions on some tasks.

[00:09:12] Diego: Yep, quantization quality depends on calibration data and where you quantize (weights only vs activations). We recommend a staged approach: weights-only int8, eval on your critical prompt set, then explore activation quantization. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles based on your evals.

[00:09:40] Priya: Quick demo note — when you run NVTX traces you'll see many micro-kernels. We correlate those with flame graphs and provide a kernel-selection suggestion: fuse or split depending on sequence length distribution.

[00:09:58] Ravi: For our deployment, the constraint is deterministic 95th latency under 200ms for <=64 token requests. Is that achievable on A100 with TRT-LLM + CUDA graphs?

[00:10:12] Diego: Likely yes if you reserve capacity and maintain warmed graphs for the common shapes. On shared clusters without reserved capacity, variance increases. That's where Redwood Dedicated helps — predictable throughput and reserved GPU pools.

[00:10:30] Omar: Any caveats for VPC/on-prem? Network NVidia drivers, container runtimes?

[00:10:38] Diego: The main dependencies are driver/CUDA/cuDNN versions, TensorRT version, and kernel module compatibility. For CUDA Graphs and CUPTI capture, certain driver versions are recommended. We'll share a validated stack matrix. For on-prem air-gapped installs we provide an installer and offline packages; KMS integration requires network to your KMS endpoints or HSM connector.

[00:11:05] Sam: How intrusive are model changes? We iterate models weekly.

[00:11:10] Diego: Model churn impacts compilation cost for TRT-LLM. We support incremental compilation and cached artifacts. For fast iteration, vLLM path gives faster deploy times but slightly worse 95p for very short prompts. Many customers use CI to precompile new model versions into graphs.

[00:11:30] Maya: Let's look at a real trace we ran with a 50/50 mix short/long: (shares graph) you can see TRT path dominating short request latency; vLLM path has better sustained throughput when long requests dominate.

[00:11:55] Ravi: Are there any open-source tooling you recommend for CUPTI/NVTX analysis?

[00:12:01] Diego: Nsight Systems, Nsight Compute, and our internal scripts which synthesize CUPTI into a per-request table. We'll share those scripts as examples.

[00:12:20] Lina: If we move to dedicated Redwood, do you still recommend hybrid routing or a single path?

[00:12:28] Diego: Hybrid often gives the best economics: low-latency path for front-door chat, high-throughput path for batch/long runs. If you can afford extreme optimization and have stable shapes, fully TRT-LLM + warmed CUDA graphs could work, but it's brittle with model churn.

[00:12:50] Priya: A quick note on metrics — we instrument per-kernel latency, memory high-water, graph warm count, and KV hits. We attach tracing ids to requests so you can correlate app-level 95p to kernel-level events.

[00:13:10] Omar: Pricing question briefly — how much extra for on-prem support and offline packages?

[00:13:18] Maya: We'll send the enterprise pricing sheet; there's a platform fee for Private plus optional managed support. I'll follow up.

[00:13:28] Ravi: Good. For the joint benchmark, how do we run it? We prefer using our on-prem cluster to see realistic memory behavior.

[00:13:36] Diego: We can run a 2-day pilot. Week 1: Redwood runs profiling scripts to collect NVTX + CUPTI on your hardware (we can run the agents in your VPC or you can share traces). Week 2: joint run of TRT-LLM vs vLLM paths with same prompt set and traffic shape. Deliverables: NVTX/CUPTI traces, kernel-level breakdown, recommended routing config, and cost/latency tradeoff doc.

[00:14:05] Sam: Do you need admin access to nodes?

[00:14:08] Diego: For live profiling it's easiest with an agent; otherwise we can give you a self-contained script and instructions to run and upload traces.

[00:14:20] Lina: Also we'll need SOC2 docs and network diagrams.

[00:14:25] Maya: I'll attach the security pack and a network diagram template after the call.

[00:14:33] Ravi: One more technical — how do you handle multi-GPU KV across model parallelism? We might want tensor-slicing for very large models.

[00:14:42] Diego: Our runtime supports both data-parallel and tensor-sliced model parallelism. KV is sharded accordingly. For tensor-parallel models we coordinate KV exchange across NVLink or PCIe; that adds latency so we often prefer model partitioning strategies that minimize cross-GPU KV traffic. We can show you latencies for NVLink vs PCIe configs.

[00:15:05] Maya: Wrapping up — quick recap of action items and next steps.

[00:15:10] Ravi: Sounds good.

[00:15:12] (end of detailed transcript capture, remainder are quick clarifying Qs and wrap)

[00:45:00] Lina: Clarify the recommended sequence-length buckets for graphs?

[00:45:10] Diego: Start with {32, 64, 128, 512} — these map to common chat and long form sizes. Warm per-bucket graphs and monitor hit rates.

[00:46:00] Ravi: Will you share an example config for hybrid routing?

[00:46:12] Maya: Yes, we'll include a sample policy file and the routing rules in the follow-up.

[00:56:30] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up on the artifacts and schedule the pilot. End call.
